sections.h2: What should I know before selling a house in Randolph?
sections.html:
Randolph Township requires a fire inspection for the sale of a one- or two-family house, and appointments fill up fast because the Fire Prevention Bureau holds them in a single weekly morning window. Book the slot as soon as you have a closing date.

Randolph is a 21-square-mile Morris County township with a high owner-occupancy rate, so owner-occupied houses make up most of the market. Whether you list, sell privately or accept an as-is cash purchase, the inspection and the deed recorded in Morristown apply to the house.

The 2025 estimate is 26,878 residents in 9,110 households. Owners live in 77.8 percent of homes, and 91.7% of residents stayed at the same address over the prior year. The median owned home is valued at $670,700, owners with a loan pay about $3,711 a month, and median household income is $175,000.

The Certificate of Smoke Detector, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Secondary Power Source Identification applies to the sale, rental or change of occupancy of a one- or two-family dwelling and comes from the New Jersey Uniform Fire Code. The Fire Official's office takes bookings on 973-989-7039, and inspections run Monday mornings from 9:30 to 11:30.

Randolph fire inspection fees

First inspection$100

Inspection requested on another day$150

The standards differ by the age of the house:

  • Every level needs a smoke detector, including the basement, with one in the hall outside each bedroom and none more than about 10 feet from a bedroom.
  • Homes built before 1977 may use battery detectors, but changeable-battery units are no longer accepted, so choose sealed 10-year batteries.
  • Homes built in 1977 or later, or with a substantial addition, must keep their hard-wired detectors working and interconnected, and may not replace them with battery types.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm goes outside the bedrooms on each level that has them.
  • A central station alarm system must work fully, including battery backup, with sounders loud enough to reach each bedroom at 70 decibels with the door closed.

sections.h2: Secondary power label and other paperwork
sections.html:
A house with generators, solar panels or battery storage must carry a label within 18 inches of the main electrical panel and meter. It reads similar to "CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER" and cannot be handwritten. A label that meets ANSI Z535.4 satisfies the rule. Put one up before the inspector arrives, and photograph it for your records.

The township fee schedule also lists a letter stating that a certificate of occupancy is not required for a change of title. Ask the Building Department whether your sale qualifies for that letter and what it costs now.

Randolph sits in the New Jersey Highlands, with ridges and valleys, and land ranging from 551 to 1,120 feet above sea level. If your lot is on a slope or beside a stream, collect any drainage or retaining wall records before listing. If the house uses a well or septic system, ask the township and county offices which records a buyer's lender will want.

Randolph maintains 119.53 of its 144.95 miles of roadway, with Morris County responsible for 19.62 miles and the state for 5.80, so confirm who maintains the road in front of your house if a buyer asks. Several towns were carved out of Randolph over the years, including Dover, Wharton, Mine Hill and Victory Gardens, so check that a plat or survey names the right municipality. Your attorney or title agent can confirm the block and lot before the deed is drafted, which avoids a rejected recording at the Registry.

sections.h2: State transfer fee and Morris County recording
sections.html:
The seller pays the state realty transfer fee. For consideration above $350,000, the Division of Taxation lists $5.30 per $500 for the portion from $550,000 to $850,000, which covers the area around Randolph's $670,700 median value.

Deeds go to the Morris County Clerk's Registry department, which is open from 8:00 am to 4:00 pm. Every land document needs a cover sheet and a cover letter with the submitter's name and address. Each document must also carry "Record and Return" or "Cancel and Return" instructions, and a return envelope should be large enough for the deed. The Registry's phone is 973-285-6130.

sections.h2: Getting through the Randolph inspection step by step
sections.html:
Call the Fire Official's office once you have a closing date and ask for a Monday slot between 9:30 and 11:30. Since only one weekly window exists, a missed slot can cost you a week.

Before the visit, check each level for a smoke detector, confirm a carbon monoxide alarm sits outside the bedrooms, and test the central station system if the house has one. Use the year of construction to decide whether battery units are acceptable. Keep the township's guidance on smoke detector placement handy while you walk through. Add the secondary power label if you have solar panels, a generator or battery storage.

If the house fails, fix the items and book the reinspection at $100. Ask the Building Department about the letter on certificates of occupancy for a change of title, and have your attorney or title agent confirm the Morris County recording steps before closing.

sections.h2: Which sale route fits a Randolph owner?
sections.html:
A listing makes sense when the house is in good shape and you have a few months. Plan for a clean inspection report from the first visit and a closing date that allows for the Monday morning slot.

An as-is cash sale shifts repair risk to the buyer. You still need the inspection certificate, so compare which party orders it and who pays a failed visit's reinspection. If tenants live in the house, remember that the same certificate applies to rentals and changes of occupancy.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and the string of repair requests that often follow a buyer's home inspection. That matters most when you must move by a set date. Ask for the offer in writing, confirm who handles the recording paperwork at the Morris County Clerk's Registry, and make sure the offer reflects the state realty transfer fee you will owe at closing. Pricing in a township where most homes are owner-occupied means comparing with nearby sales, so ask for recent closed prices before you decide.

faqs.q: Does Randolph require an inspection when I sell my house?
faqs.a: Yes. A smoke detector, carbon monoxide alarm and secondary power source certificate is needed for the sale of a one- or two-family dwelling. The Randolph Fire Prevention Bureau performs it.

faqs.q: How much does the Randolph fire inspection cost?
faqs.a: The first inspection is $100 and each reinspection is $100. An inspection requested on another day costs $150. Appointments run Monday mornings from 9:30 to 11:30 and fill up quickly.

faqs.q: Can I use battery smoke detectors in my Randolph house?
faqs.a: Only in some cases. Homes built before 1977 may use battery units, and they must have sealed 10-year batteries. Homes built in 1977 or later, or with a substantial addition, must keep hard-wired interconnected detectors working.

faqs.q: Where is a Randolph deed recorded?
faqs.a: The Morris County Clerk's Registry department records it, with a cover sheet attached to the document. Registry recording hours are 8:00 am to 4:00 pm.

faqs.q: What transfer fee applies to a Randolph sale near the median home value?
faqs.a: The seller pays the state realty transfer fee. A $670,700 sale falls between $550,000 and $850,000, where the Division of Taxation schedule lists $5.30 per $500 for that portion of the price.
